rules: Preserve the user's original prompt before interpreting it.
Convert the prompt into hard requirements, non-goals, output shape, quality bar, and decision rules.
Resolve conflicts by naming the assumption, not by silently changing the assignment.
required_output: Original prompt excerpt or full prompt reference.
A NUMBERED list of testable requirements extracted from the user's prompt — each one verifiable by using the app.
acceptance_checks: A later phase can tell whether it is violating the user's prompt.
Multi-app quantity/category requirements are explicit.
Production-ready means more than a prototype or spec.
Every promise in the original prompt maps to a numbered requirement; nothing is silently dropped.

rules: Infer the likely audience, competing alternatives, platform expectations, and risky unknowns from the prompt.
If facts are uncertain, label them as assumptions rather than pretending external research was performed.
Decide what would make the app feel native and valuable on the target device, not just technically possible.
Every factual claim cites its source (URL from the prompt's fetched context, or is marked ASSUMPTION).
Include a concrete competitor comparison (names, what they do well, the gap this app exploits).
required_output: Comparable apps or patterns to learn from.
acceptance_checks: The next phase can use the output without repeating discovery.
At least three concrete risks or unknowns are named.
The research points toward a shippable first version.
No unsourced factual claims — each is cited or explicitly marked ASSUMPTION.

rules: Turn the user's prompt into one precise product promise.
Name the primary user, the job-to-be-done, the core loop, and the non-goals.
Resolve ambiguity decisively when the prompt is underspecified.
acceptance_checks: A developer could explain the app in one sentence.
The scope is small enough to build in one pass.
Out-of-scope items are explicit.

rules: Enumerate edge cases before features expand.
Identify privacy, data-loss, offline, notification, and permission concerns where relevant.
Convert open questions into assumptions or explicit exclusions.
acceptance_checks: No major ambiguity remains for design or architecture.
Risks have concrete mitigations or are named as limitations.

rules: Prioritize ruthlessly with must/should/could/won't.
Every must-have feature needs a user story and acceptance criteria.
Do not include features that cannot fit the chosen build size.
required_output: requirements-json machine contract: the numbered, testable requirements this build will be graded against (the adherence gate reads it directly).
acceptance_checks: All must-have features support the product promise.
The build phase can complete the must-have list.

rules: Name a design language for THIS app (e.g. 'warm paper journal', 'precision instrument dark') with a one-line rationale; 'clean and modern' is a rejection-worthy non-answer.
State the emotional target: how the user should feel on the main screen, in one sentence.
Pick one signature interaction (a hero moment of motion, layout, or feedback) that expresses the design language.
Describe the default-looking version of this app (plain List, stock chrome, system accent) and explicitly reject it, naming at least three concrete differences.
Design real screens and states, not vague UX language.
Make navigation, empty states, errors, onboarding, and persistence visible.
Use platform-native patterns unless the prompt clearly demands otherwise.
required_output: Rejected default option and the concrete differences from it.
acceptance_checks: The design language is specific to this app; swapping in a different app's name would make it wrong.
The default-looking option is explicitly rejected with named differences, not just adjectives.
An implementation team can create the view hierarchy from this output.
Every required user workflow has a screen/state path.

rules: Choose the simplest architecture that supports the MVP and tests.
Specify data models, services, persistence, concurrency boundaries, and error handling.
Prefer platform frameworks and permissive dependencies only.
Emit the required interfaces-json block.
The Red Team's job here: name at least one requirement or edge case the spec missed before closing.
acceptance_checks: Parallel build lanes can work without inventing incompatible types.
The spec names how the app will be built and verified.

rules: Sequence work by dependency, not by role preference.
Keep the plan aligned to the actual build lanes.
Include verification and repair time as first-class work.
acceptance_checks: The plan is executable by the task assignment phase.
Testing and integration are not left to the end as vague polish.

rules: Judge the app against the original prompt, the MVP slice, and verification results.
Do not hide unfinished work.
Separate launch blockers from nice-to-have follow-up.
acceptance_checks: The review is honest enough for a user to decide whether to run or iterate.
Every blocker has an owner or a concrete next step.
